task.description:
WF-03 Step 2 -- design the fix for ISS-0440. Produce a design artefact under lib/letflow/design/ (suggested iss440-handoff-status-enforcement.md). Design only, NO implementation code.

READ ISSUE-FIXER's Step 1 diagnosis FIRST (artifacts_in[0]). It did real empirical work and CORRECTED two facts ORCH supplied at Step 00 -- treat its findings as the evidence base, but per HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md 1.1 verify what your design leans on.

THE ESTABLISHED EVIDENCE:
  - EIGHT occurrences, not seven (this run's own trigger is the 8th), across SEVEN DISTINCT ROLES (TEST-DESIGN-VALIDATOR, TEST-RUNNER x2, RELEASE-VALIDATOR, CODE-DESIGNER, SECURITY-REVIEWER, REVIEWER, ELIXIR-DEV), none repeating more than twice. This is SYSTEMIC, not a single-role problem -- a fix targeting one role's prompt cannot work.
  - ORCH has NEVER been the offender. Every violation was written by the COMPLETING agent at step completion. That asymmetry is load-bearing: it is why an ORCH-side check is an INDEPENDENT second reader rather than asking the error-prone party to self-check.
  - Bad-value vocabulary: DONE x4, PASS x2, COMPLETE x1, FAIL x1.
  - TIMING, corrected: the linter's 8.4s is the QUIET-HOST number. ISSUE-FIXER measured 74.7s once, under 3 concurrent erl processes from other worktrees on this same checkout. A 9-15x slowdown under contention IS the real operating condition on this workstation (multiple concurrent sessions are normal here). AC5 must be judged against the contended number, not the quiet one. ORCH independently confirms concurrent sessions are routine.
  - run(_args) at lint_handoffs.ex:233 ignores its arguments and always lints the full corpus. No single-file mode exists. Any per-dispatch or per-file gate needs one built.
  - ORCH independently scanned all 1899 handoff JSONs: ZERO bad string values present today. Every past occurrence was fixed. So this design is purely about PREVENTING RECURRENCE, not cleaning up existing debt -- do not design a corpus migration.
  - No prior issue (ISS-0190/0191/0196/0198/0203/0204/0262) rejected any of the four candidates, so none is foreclosed by a decision record.

THE AUTOFIX AMBIGUITY -- ISSUE-FIXER resolved this empirically and your design MUST respect the result. Every recoverable historical fix mapped PASS/COMPLETE/DONE -> COMPLETED with zero counterexamples. But the single historical top-level FAIL is squash-merged out of recoverable history, so whether it should have become FAILED (lifecycle) or COMPLETED (a finished step with a failing result) CANNOT be determined. Therefore: an autofix may handle {PASS, COMPLETE, DONE} -> COMPLETED, and MUST REFUSE -- not guess -- on FAIL. Silently converting a genuinely FAILED handoff to COMPLETED would corrupt the pipeline's own record of what happened, which is worse than the violation. If your design includes autofix, state this refusal behaviour explicitly and say what the refusal looks like to the caller.

THE PROPERTY THAT MUST HOLD -- this is the heart of the design. ISSUE-FIXER named it: the check must fire as a MECHANICAL CONSEQUENCE OF AN ACTION THE PIPELINE CANNOT AVOID TAKING, with ZERO agent decision about whether to run it. All six prior mitigations were prose asking someone to remember, and all six failed. Your design must state, explicitly, which unavoidable action its enforcement rides on, and why that action cannot be skipped. A design whose answer is 'the agent runs the linter' or 'ORCH remembers to check' is the seventh failed mitigation and will be rejected.
  ISSUE-FIXER's recommendation, which you may adopt, refine, or reject with reasoning: restricted autofix (handles 3 of the 4 bad values with no agent action, riding CI's existing unconditional gate) PLUS candidate (b) wired into ORCH's EXISTING commit-at-dispatch mechanism -- the same precedent shape as ISS-0196 / HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md 1.3, which has held since it was adopted. That precedent matters: 1.3 works because committing the handoff is something ORCH already unavoidably does.

ASSESS THE HOOK OPTION HONESTLY. ISSUE-FIXER proved a .githooks/pre-push works mechanically but noted (i) an unconfigured host has ZERO protection, (ii) no existing check_* task verifies hook setup so one would have to be built, and (iii) such a task could only run inside mix letflow.check -- which already catches 100% of these at CI anyway, making the added task nearly circular. AC2 demands that an unconfigured host either still be protected or have its non-setup detected by an existing gate. If you propose the hook, answer AC2 head-on. If you reject it, say so and why -- rejecting a listed option with stated reasoning is a legitimate design outcome.

ADDRESS ALL FIVE ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA in docs/issues/ISS-0440.yaml explicitly, especially AC1 (the mechanism must catch a DELIBERATELY-INTRODUCED bad status BEFORE CI, demonstrated by a real run) -- state how a validator will demonstrate that, and AC5 (the cost question) against the CONTENDED timing.

SELF-REFERENTIAL OPPORTUNITY worth using: this run's own handoffs are written by the very agents that produce these violations, and are checked by the very linter being changed. Your design can specify that the fix be demonstrated against this run's own handoff files. A fix that cannot catch a violation planted in its own run's handoffs has not been shown to work.

Deliverable: the design document plus a complete handoff (artifacts_out naming the design path, next_action routing to CODE-DESIGN-VALIDATOR). Commit both to branch feature/WF03-ISS0440-20260903.

result.summary:
Design written to lib/letflow/design/iss440-handoff-status-enforcement.md. Verified (not inherited) before building on it: mix.exs's letflow.check alias (lines 91-108) is a fixed, unconditional list with letflow.lint_handoffs already present, ahead of format/compile/test; .github/workflows/ci.yml's backend job's only content step is `run: mix letflow.check`, no flags, no conditional -- this is the strongest unavoidable action in the pipeline, since it requires zero per-host setup (runs on GitHub's own runner). Also verified lint_handoffs.ex:233-234 (run(_args) truly ignores its argument today), the @grandfathered list (no H1 entries currently grandfathered), and confirmed via `git worktree list` that 3 other worktrees are live on this checkout right now -- independent corroboration of the contended-concurrency premise.

THE UNAVOIDABLE ACTIONS (the design's core answer): (1) mix letflow.check runs on every push/PR via CI's own trigger, not agent choice, and GIT_MERGE.md's CI-green gate already makes it a hard merge precondition -- Mechanism A (restricted --autofix) rides this, needing no new call site. (2) HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md section 1.3's dispatch-time handoff commit is already unconditional, no size threshold, no judgement gate, and has held with a clean record since ISS-0196 -- Mechanism B inserts a status-field read as an inseparable numbered clause of that SAME existing procedure (not a new standalone step), positioned before the existing commit step, so there is no path through the procedure that reaches the commit without passing the read. Verified all 8 occurrences were written by the completing agent, never by ORCH authoring its own handoff -- so Mechanism B asks a party with a clean record (ORCH, reading fresh) to catch a party that has never once caught itself, rather than asking the error-prone party to self-check (candidate (c)'s flaw).

VERDICT ON THE FOUR CANDIDATES: (a) tracked .githooks/pre-push -- REJECTED as a required mechanism. Proven mechanically live (design section 4a), but AC2 fails for it standalone: an unconfigured host gets zero protection, no existing check_* task verifies hook setup, and building one could only run inside mix letflow.check -- i.e. inside the very CI gate that already independently catches 100% of these regardless of hooks, making a hook-setup-verifier circular. Its only real value (faster local feedback on a configured host) is real but small, needs new tracked infra, and conflicts with this project's own instruction not to touch .git/hooks or git config on this shared, concurrently-used checkout. Recorded as an optional future pure-addition on top of A+B, not adopted now. (b) ORCH lints before dispatching -- ADOPTED, refined into Mechanism B: not literally 'call mix letflow.lint_handoffs at every dispatch' (too costly under the contended 74.7s figure, and over-general), but a single string-equality field read against 6 literals, costing nothing measurable against either timing figure, wired into section 1.3's existing procedure. (c) lint call in every role's dispatch template -- REJECTED: asks the exact party proven error-prone (the completing agent, all 8/8 occurrences) to self-check immediately after erring, structurally weaker than (b)/Mechanism B's independent-reader shape; also a larger, more error-prone edit surface (~15 role files vs. one procedure doc). (d) --autofix -- ADOPTED, restricted: closed map {PASS,COMPLETE,DONE} -> COMPLETED only (matches 100% of independently-verifiable historical fixes, 0 counterexamples), MUST REFUSE on FAIL or any unrecognized value -- refusal leaves the file untouched, still counts as a hard violation, and reports the file/value/reason distinctly from a silent pass, exactly because the one historical FAIL instance is squash-merged out of recoverable history and the lifecycle-vs-result-shape question cannot be verified either way for it.

AC1 (catch before CI, demonstrated by a real run): satisfied twice over -- Mechanism B catches it before CI even runs (at ORCH's pre-dispatch commit point); Mechanism A catches/self-heals it at CI's own existing hard gate. Demonstration path specified in design section 5/AC1: ELIXIR-DEV's test suite plants a deliberately-bad top-level status (PASS, then FAIL) into a SCRATCH COPY/fixture (never a real handoffs/ file), runs mix letflow.lint_handoffs (flags it, non-zero exit) and mix letflow.lint_handoffs --autofix (rewrites PASS, refuses FAIL with the stated message and still-nonzero exit) against it, quoting real output -- using this run's own self-referential opportunity (a fixture modeled on this run's own handoff shape) per the handoff's own instruction. AC2 (unconfigured host): satisfied by construction, not by a new detection task -- Mechanism A requires zero per-host setup because it rides CI, which runs identically for every host regardless of local configuration; 'unconfigured' is not a state that exists for this mechanism, which is the stated reason the hook was not adopted as required. AC3 (mapping must not corrupt the record): satisfied by the closed map + explicit refuse-and-report contract in design section 2.2-2.3. AC4 (systemic, not role-scoped): satisfied structurally -- neither mechanism reads to_agent/from_agent at all. AC5 (cost vs. the CONTENDED 74.7s figure): Mechanism A adds zero new linter call sites (reuses CI's existing single invocation); Mechanism B never invokes the linter at all (in-memory field read on a file already in hand) -- the 74.7s figure is precisely why this design avoids the literal 'lint at every dispatch' reading of (b)/(c), which is rejected/refined away from in design sections 3.3-3.4 and 4(c).

Open questions listed explicitly per this role's mandate (design section 6), not silently resolved: whether FAIL should ever become autofixable given future, non-squashed evidence (left unresolved -- ELIXIR-DEV must not extend the map to cover it under this handoff's scope); exact prose/placement of the section 1.3 procedural insertion (content specified, wording left to the implementing/doc-updating role); whether CI should self-heal via a write-back commit (explicitly out of scope -- --autofix is a local-invocable capability, NOT wired into the letflow.check alias CI calls, so CI keeps failing loudly rather than silently rewriting a PR branch mid-run; this is also why AC2's answer stays clean). No implementation code present -- verified by grep for def/defp/end-block patterns and elixir code fences in the design file; only @spec-style signatures, a closed data-shape table, and a numbered procedural description (prose, not Elixir) are present.
result.next_action: Route to CODE-DESIGN-VALIDATOR (WF-03 gate equivalent to WF-02 Step 1b)
